storytitle: The End of the Seed's Journey
text: Day 193 since leaving Granny's place. Yunguo sat by the riverbank, her chin resting in her hands. She thought about the last packet of seeds she had planted. They should be blooming by now. Maybe there would be fruit soon... It was a shame she wouldn't get to see it. The Islet where she had planted those seeds was nowhere to be found. People always leave. She vaguely understood that. Yunguo let out a long sigh and counted the Dough and produce in her bag, trying to stay hopeful. If she didn't eat or drink, she could last another five days. Still... it was so cold. She hugged her knees and buried her face in her arms, rubbing her eyes. Suddenly, everything went dark. But she felt warm, as if she were buried in soft soil. It almost felt nice, like she could just fall asleep like that. Then she heard the wind. She heard water flowing. She heard insects chirping. She saw an earthworm wriggling beside her, loosening the soil... Wait, where did that earthworm come from?!

Yunguo's face flushed deep red. She couldn't say a word. She just closed her eyes and braced herself for the storm...

But Granny only gave her head a gentle pat and sighed. "Not every seedling will grow strong just because you tend it with care. There are storms, droughts, pests... all kinds of hardship. You never know what they'll come up against. You have to face that. So do they."

The next day at school, Yunguo's group turned in a yellowing tomato seedling.
"Didn't you all want to be in her group before?"
"Hah, what kind of 'prodigy' is that?"

Blushing, yet with a hopeful spark in her eyes, Yunguo said, "W-We didn't get the result wrong... it was the process. Next time, we can fix it together."
No one replied, but that was all right.

"What's it like outside? Is it this dark too?"
Yunguo heard her own voice, as if asking someone.
"No, it's bright out there. Let me loosen the soil a bit so you can get through."
The earthworm spoke as it wriggled upward, working so hard that Yunguo was moved. But earthworms can't talk, can they? They shouldn't be able to!
"What if it's too cold outside?"
She heard herself ask again, glancing around at the warm, dark soil that surrounded her.
"There's sunlight! Once you find the sun, it won't be cold anymore."
The earthworm happily burrowed its way out, and a beam of light broke through the soil into Yunguo's eyes, almost blinding, but warm.

Yunguo woke up, still a little dazed from the nap. The river before her shimmered with the hues of the setting sun. Beside her, the phone lit up with a message from Granny: "What did you eat today?"

Almost without thinking, Yunguo typed, "Nothing yet," but her finger hovered above the send button. After a moment, she deleted it and started over: "Gonna make some congee with apples tonight. Should be yummy."

Yunguo pulled up a number from her contacts. Granny had once said it belonged to a proper grown-up who'd traveled the universe all alone. "If you ever get stuck, you go ask him."
"H-Hello... I'm Yunguo, from Mount Zhuxi. We met when I was little... I've... um... I've been livin' by myself for half a year now, and I've kinda run out of money..."

She practiced saying it aloud, but the more she thought about it, the more it felt wrong, like she was calling just to be a trouble.
"...This is my first time leavin' Granny... I came out on my own to learn how to grow things... She asked me to visit you first, and maybe get some lil' advice about livin' on my own."

After practicing over and over until she was sure she could say it smoothly, Yunguo took a deep breath and dialed the number. To her surprise, it was answered after just one ring.
"H-Hello! Mr. Mobai..."
"Huh? I'm not Mobai. This is Elsa..."

"S-Sorry!!!"
Yunguo hung up in a panic, her face turning bright red even though there was no one else around on the unfamiliar islet.
A moment later, her phone rang again. The caller ID showed "Mr. Mobai."

Mount Zhuxi was in an uproar. The chestnut vendor hollered it mid-stir to his customer. The postman, cooling off in the shade, passed it to the sugar painting artist. The repairman patching a bike tire called it out to the passing peddler— "The Yuns' kid is missing!" Did it matter whether anyone actually knew who the Yuns were? Not a bit. Just spread the word. Nothing could go wrong if everyone helped look. Blushberry — that was the kid who never smiled, the one who burst into tears the moment she saw a stranger. Granny was by the well in front of the bamboo house, washing mugwort leaves when she caught wind of it. She always boiled them in summer for the little one's bath, to keep the mosquitoes away and keep the rash at bay... Wait, who did you say was missin'? "Told you, her Gramps's no good at mindin' kids." Grabbing her palm fan, she charged down the mountain. The search party for Blushberry stirred the entire mountain. By the time the sun was about to set, everyone finally let out a breath of relief.

By the time Yunguo brought the tomato seedling home, hidden under her clothes, it was already past dinner.
At this hour, Granny would usually be chatting away in someone else's courtyard, so there was no chance of running into her—

"What are you sneaking in there?" Granny caught her red-handed, her gaze landing right on the yellowing seedling.
"You're not planning to swap this out for one you grew yourself and turn that in, are you?"

So lately, her grandparents had been carrying her around in a bamboo basket, hoping she'd get used to being around people — some kind of training or exposure or whatever they call it. But little Blushberry had never budged from the depths of her basket. The Skies Above as their witness, all anyone had seen were two fuzzy ears poking out. Now, the basket had gone quiet. Perhaps she was asleep. They decided to sneak a peek. It was empty. Empty?!

At the foot of Mount Zhuxi, along the ridges of the rice paddies, a scattering of bamboo flasks and woven baskets lined the path. The villagers, bent over the fields since dawn, were only now settling down for a well-earned sip of tea.
A joke went around that while everyone else's baskets were heavy with crops or tools, the Yuns'? Theirs carried their two-year-old granddaughter, Blushberry.

Unlike the other grey-furred toddlers, this little one looked as if a fluffy sun had tumbled into the bamboo grove — red, radiant, and bright as a ripe fruit on harvest day. A pity, though. No matter what anyone tried, she never smiled. The moment a stranger came near, she'd shrink away. And on bad days, she'd burst into loud, panicked wails.

During the ceremonial wrestling match held to honor their deity, Dorjelang sat by the lakeside and watched the spectacle of fervor and power. Out of place and even slightly dissonant with the scene was the low, chanted verses from the herder next to him: When chaos gave birth to earth and sky, White yak from the lotus did arise, With ears that hear all earthly things, Nose that scents far and wide, Wings to soar o'er mountains and rivers, Hooves to race across plains and fissures, He is the mighty mountain high, He is the gentle flowing stream, He is the father working hard, He is the mother's loving heart, He tames the strong and lifts the meek, His righteous name through ages speak, His legend in our hearts engraved, Through song we sing his ageless praise. The song spoke of the highland deity. Legend has it that "he" looked just like everyone else in the tribe, with long flowing hair, a strong athletic build, and mighty long horns, and that "he" danced to the heavens and sang for the earth. "Behold, it brings success. Behold, it's filled with fortune. And behold, it possesses the eternal..." Dorjelang caught himself humming along. He glanced at his own reflection in the emerald lake... Me? I look nothing like the deity, moo. A buddy from a neighboring tribe came over. Dorjelang could see his messy hair and his beautiful, sturdy horns that put his own feeble ones to shame. His buddy stroked his chin in deep thought.

storytitle: Over the Mountain Far From Home
text:
This was Dorjelang's sixteenth year living on the highland pastures.
Back then, he knew nothing of the world beyond.

Dorjelang was seen as someone who needed protection in his tribe. He thought if he could be a little stronger and a little tougher, put on a stern face and look a little fiercer... then maybe he would actually become more capable.
Perhaps due to his frailty, there were many things off-limits to him, like going down to the river, wrestling, or herding alone. Concerned gazes followed him around whenever he tried to get involved.
The old herder who tutored him said that his body wasn't as strong because he carried all the good fortune of the highlands on his head, that he was a child blessed by their deity.
Whenever they took him out to herd, the wolves would scatter, snowstorms would cease, and blood-sucking insects would disperse.

Dorjelang wanted to believe in it.

When he woke from the dream, the moonlit figure was gone, and next to him, there was only the foxtail hat.
His companion had kept watch under the moon, coming and departing in soft silence. No mountains or rivers, nor winds of the highlands could ever scatter the memories of its devoted silhouette.
Though years may pass, its form remains, timeless beneath the moonlight's glow.
Though the permafrost before dawn may never melt, the warmth in his heart endures.

It was the thirty-ninth day of Dorjelang's arduous journey across the endless mountains.
He stood at a station in the Starsea and glanced back at the dawn-gilded peaks of his homeland. He tucked the little foxtail hat into his luggage and moved on.
The boy, once sheltered by so many, had finally made it over the mountains.

Deep in the night by a stream, Dorjelang rested his head on his luggage and watched as Doggie snored beside him. He hadn't noticed the whites in its fur before, realizing just how old it had grown. It's only minor injuries, we'll heal soon. He told himself as he fell asleep. Wolf howls came to Dorjelang's dreams, and he tried opening his eyes. Unsure if they were actually opened, Dorjelang believed he saw Doggie on a moonlit hill with head raised to the sky. Its graying fur seemed to glow as it let out the longest unfettered cry in its life, and the woods answered with an echoing chorus of wolfsong.

Unable to convince Doggie to leave, Dorjelang could only watch as it busied itself with scouting the path ahead, lagging behind, catching up again, and panting breathlessly with stalks of foxtail in its mouth, and even a rabbit... Wait, drop that right now! Strange, this was supposed to be a journey that took them farther and farther away from home, but with Doggie's company, every day, he felt blessed with luck like all the days before. Still, danger and uncertainty drew ever closer, and when he picked up the dull cracking sounds echoing through the quiet mountains, he knew an avalanche was coming. By the time he woke up between a slush of mud and snow, he had no idea how long he'd been buried. A wet tongue licked his eyes, blurring the moon in his vision, and under it, he saw Doggie whimpering and digging through the snow. So the deity has blessed me after all! he thought and smiled, not daring to make a sound for fear of stirring the mountain again. Doggie had suffered a broken hind leg and a gash on its scalp. Dorjelang applied some medicinal herbs to the wound and grabbed some foxtail to weave a little hat, so as to keep Doggie from scratching its head. Holding his companion, Dorjelang thought about turning back to their village, but the way back was even longer than continuing forward. Doggie barked furiously in protest, as if to say, "All my work would have been for nothing if you turned back now." Man and dog then traveled even farther.

As time passed, Dorjelang grew up to be the weakest in the tribe, while Doggie became the alpha of the canines. However, the herders had always suspected that Doggie was actually a grassland wolf.

Whenever Doggie tried to howl, Dorjelang would gently hold his muzzle shut, worried that he might leave with a wolf pack that picked up the call.

Doggie's name was simply Doggie. He stayed by Dorjelang's side through everything like a faithful guardian — herding with him, wrestling with him, accompanying him on pilgrimages to mountain tops...
Even now, he wanted to keep Dorjelang company on his journey away from home.

It was the ninth day of Dorjelang's arduous journey across the endless mountains.
He had prepared himself for the inevitable solitude that came with leaving home, but as he woke from a dream, he found a figure basking under the moon.

Doggie, his childhood companion, had secretly followed him. He was grinning and lolling his tongue, as if to say, "Took you long enough to notice me."

The old herders used to tell the story of how a flood once swept little Dorjelang out of the shed where he'd been sunbathing. When they finally found him, Doggie was whimpering, and Dorjelang was crying even louder.

The two little ones had just opened their eyes and were wrestling each other under an ownerless hat. Everyone thought they'd go their separate ways, but some bonds, once formed, could only deepen.

Dorjelang kept his serious face as he pondered how someone so little could exude such immense presence. The lengthy silence between them irritated the smaller one, and she jumped up and smacked Dorjelang right on his head.

"Who are you trying to bluff with that hat? I'll give you credit for helping with the light pole, but now you've got to pay for my walls!"

The smack snapped Dorjelang out of it. He adjusted his hat and bowed humbly as he patted his chest.

"This is my fault, and I'll take full responsibility!" he said.

This was Dorjelang's first day at the Galactic Bazaar.
It was also the day he first met Master Mufflin, and surprisingly, he didn't need to become stronger. He just needed to appear more approachable. 
That's when he took off the fierce-looking hat of his and changed how he interacted with and saw the world around him, starting with working to pay off the damage he'd caused.
He came here for a reason... but he couldn't remember what.

"They say not to mind what others think, but that's easier said than done. 'Hearing' is a way for us to feel the world," he said.
A hat with solid long horns was then placed on Dorjelang's head.
"HAHMM! Now you look like a tough guy! Put on the hat, and you can become whoever you want to be. Come on, show us your angry face!"
In the lake's reflection, Dorjelang did look quite mighty! And just like that, the kid was fooled by his buddy.

Frightened by their fear, Dorjelang fled in panic, accidentally bumping into something as he ran...
Amidst the rising dust, dizzy and disoriented, Dorjelang saw a massive figure approaching. He could barely contain his excitement at the prospect of meeting someone like himself.

The dust settled, but Dorjelang didn't see anyone.
"Tsk! Tsk tsk! Who?! Who broke down the walls of my workshop?..."
Dorjelang looked down and saw a little one wearing a white feather scarf. She looked up at him judgingly.
"You again?"

It was Dorjelang's first day at the Galactic Bazaar. All his life, he had felt adrift in a vast sea of people — without direction, without a place to belong. After hauling five boxes of goods for a shopkeeper at the street corner, it suddenly occurred to him that everyone here was so small, and he was incredibly strong in comparison... Maybe... I can actually help them? The revelation filled him with unprecedented joy and the urge to act, but he must stay calm. A slight turn of his body was enough to send someone flying... Mmmooo? Wasn't someone here just now? After eight victims, six cracked chairs, four shattered steps, and three flattened billboards, all eyes were trained on him with terror. He spent all his money making amends, then hurried through every intersection, anxiously avoiding anyone who came too close. Finally, he found a quiet corner to settle in. Crouching down, he took a deep breath and reminded himself to exercise more self-restraint. When he lifted his head again, he realized he was at a high point in the bazaar. Following the sound of music, he saw cheerful crowds, lively stages, and a shimmering magician's tent below...

Dorjelang had once been small and fragile, the kind who stayed tucked behind others, always in need of protection. But everyone in the workshop had seen him, without meaning to, snap table legs, crush teacups, and crack plates... so they could only assume the gentle giant had been far too modest about his strength. To Dorjelang, being able to use that strength to help those weaker than himself was a kind of luck he held dear. It had nothing to do with meeting anyone's expectations. It simply meant that when he wanted to help, he could. Master Mufflin, however, insisted he had yet to understand. She watched him as he left and remembered how her bright-eyed student dug her out of a pile of magazines in the basement five years ago... No, scratch that part. She had been standing atop that very pile, arms folded, quizzing him on hats, while he answered every question with ease. Learning on his own, in secret? How dare he?! In her irritation, she leapt down and twisted her ankle... No, scratch that part too. By the magazine pile, Dorjelang had been weaving with reeds, recreating every hat on those pages. The audacity to learn in secret... She turned away with a scowl. Even so, Dorjelang had earned approval with a "Be here at eight tomorrow morning." For him, it brought a different kind of joy and anticipation, something he didn't feel when helping others. Five years had passed since Dorjelang became a hat-making apprentice. On this day, he chose a dandelion to adorn the hat meant to welcome spring. With his new kit slung over his back, he set out once more. He still dreamed of the past — of jagged mountain paths strewn with stone, of snow and forests, of winds that never ceased, and of foxtail grass swaying gently in their wake. The dandelion lifted in the breeze and drifted toward distant mountains, as if gathering those dreams. He wondered who it would stir awake this time.

Unable to bear it any longer, Mufflin hopped down from the parapet in frustration.
On the ground, she stood a full five heads shorter than him, yet her sharp, rapid-fire scolding gave her an almost towering presence. She launched into a tirade, rattling off every misstep of his apprenticeship, from the six times he had smashed into walls over the past five years to the overly neat pile of yarn from the night before.

"You're a hatmaker! Stop wasting your time on trivial things, and go think about why we make hats!"

Dorjelang scratched his head sheepishly and nodded, which only irritated his master further, her white feather scarf slipping askew.

Shortly after, Dorjelang sat obediently by the rooftop grill, his limbs tucked in. Across from him, Master Mufflin stood with her arms crossed, glaring down at her student.
"How long have you been my student?" she demanded. But before he could answer, she jabbed a finger at his nose. "Five years! It's about time you graduated!"

Dorjelang didn't respond. His expression stayed grave as he sank into thought, and, as always, an awkward silence stretched between them.

Just as he finished, a passing senior, buried beneath a stack of fresh fabric, casually hollered for Dorjelang to help carry the load. The cook followed, smiling as she hooked two buckets of sweet soup onto his arms for a quick delivery to the canteen. Dorjelang nodded solemnly at every request, yet a glint in his eyes betrayed a secret pride. It was clear he relished the weight of such responsibilities. Up on the rooftop, Master Mufflin was snacking on roasted silkworm cocoons. Watching the big oaf dash back and forth across the yard, she clicked her tongue in irritation and stripped the skewer clean in one bite. Flick. The skewer shot forward and struck Dorjelang squarely in the back before bouncing away. He scratched the spot in confusion, then tilted his head up toward the rooftop.

This was Dorjelang's fifth year as a hat-making apprentice.
By the window, he studied the two fabric flowers in his hands with quiet intensity, weighing which one would better suit a hat meant to welcome the spring.

Suddenly, a cry for help rang out from a senior apprentice in the courtyard. A harsh gust of wind had swept the drying materials into a chaotic, tumbling flurry. With a thunderous rumble of footsteps, Dorjelang charged out. His colossal frame seemed to blot out the sun as he dashed across the yard, scooping every last stray piece into his arms in one swift rush.

This place probably isn't right for him... Dorjelang scratched his head nervously and shook it. No, it wasn't about fitting in. He left home to find his buddy and bring him back.

Dorjelang looked at the stage again as another group of laughing performers took their turn. This was the world of dreams and aspirations that his buddy lived in. Would he even want to return with him at all?

Lost in thought, Dorjelang found himself drawn closer to the stage. The mesmerizing lights kept shifting, and no one noticed when one of the light poles started to wobble.
He instinctively caught the falling pole, but when he turned around, he saw countless fearful, confused eyes staring at him, as if trying to see right through his otherness.

In this world, he could easily destroy everything with a slight movement of his hand.
His turquoise beads, horned barbaric hat, towering build, and thunderous voice... everything about him struck fear in others.
He realized then that being powerful and mighty wasn't something to be proud of after all.

The first among them to think of leaving was his buddy. Pulling Dorjelang along, he made grand plans of how he would conquer the endless mountains and see the world beyond in pursuit of his dreams. Dreams? What are... dreams? Buddies stick together till the end, so you're coming too, Dorjelang. Dorjelang was worried that he'd hold his buddy back, being as frail as he was. But his friend had unwavering faith in him. Before they left, his buddy got caught "loaning" a couple of barley buns from an old herder. Dorjelang went for the rescue, but froze at the doorway. "HAHMM? You have no right to keep him on the pastures forever..." On the glimmering highlands where heaven is just a few steps away, too many struggle to make the journey because of a weighted heart. "You've never believed in him. You just think he's weak, and needs protection..." Outside the house, Dorjelang listened as Doggie came over. As always, it sat beside him, panting with a lolling tongue, as if saying, "Eavesdropping too, huh?" "How long will you deceive him with these words? Are you going to keep sheltering him his whole life?" Dorjelang gazed up at the sunset's glow, at the deity watching over the highlands. "There is no divine blessing. He has the same horns and fur on his head as us, plus a yak horn hat that I traded with barley buns..." Please let all my good fortune rest upon my buddy's head— "I have my own dreams and my own path to follow, so I won't stay... but save half the barley bun for him. I'm leaving this place..." May he be safe, free, and prosperous on the journey of his dreams. This was Dorjelang's sixteenth year living on the highland pastures. In the empty house his buddy left behind, the old herder threw him a bundle of supplies, his mustache bristling with anger. He told Dorjelang to get out there and bring back his good-for-nothing buddy. Finally, he understood there was a kind of longing in this world that words cannot capture. He wanted to cross this mountain, and the next one beyond, and countless more after.

It was another day, ten years ago.
After finishing the night patrol, young Msafiri sneaked behind the tent again and, imitating his mother, picked up a stone and scratched a few wobbly triangles on the ground. His attempts almost seemed pitiful when compared to his mother's refined string of shapes.

That made him curious as to how exactly she managed to draw such straight lines. As he carefully traced those lines with his stone, he caught a sudden "thud" from behind — his toddler brother had fallen. With a body that reacted faster than his mind, young Msafiri turned and rushed to scoop up his brother, not realizing that the beautiful triangles had been cut in half by a long, grave scratch. "HISS!" Caught in the moment, young Msafiri couldn't tell if his father was angry or simply concerned. Maybe it was his loud hisses, or maybe it was the hypnotic dance of the campfire... either way, Msafiri couldn't remember what exactly happened after. He vaguely recalled his mother telling him a story while pointing at the stars in the sky. A story about those geometric patterns. Perhaps it was time to visit home after this expedition? It had been long since he last went back. But for now, Msafiri felt his eyelids grow heavy and allowed the night to gently shut his eyes. Just a brief nap... a micro-nap that won't do any harm, he comforted himself. Frost began to form on top of his lashes as they quivered in the wind, but the bonfire in his dreams was simply so warm that he didn't want to wake up. "Once upon a time..." He could hear his mother's gentle voice again, but it jolted him awake instead. Reflected in his bright pupils, several stars in the dark sky formed the shape he knew by heart and blinked to a pulse, as if responding to some query.

It was an evening ten years ago. "One, two, three..." "One, two, three, four, five..." Young Msafiri, who had just learned to count, was squatting on the ground and enthusiastically tracing the geometric patterns his mother had drawn around their camp. Three points, in groups of five — he shared the pattern he discovered with his little brother, who was still too young to speak. His brother tilted his head and twitched his ears, listening intently even if he didn't understand a word. The tantalizing smell of roasted meat from the campfire teased young Msafiri's nose, and his empty stomach growled shamelessly in protest. Nope, no food until I learn this! he silently vowed. ... Msafiri twitched his ears and wrinkled his nose as the memories came. The wild winds indiscriminately assaulted all in its path, chilling travelers to the bone. It had been three days and three nights, and Msafiri still hadn't tracked down any prey. The memories of roasted meat could no longer make him salivate. Forget about exploring the planet under these conditions — it was much more likely for him to end up a desiccated corpse and become one with this wilderness. Msafiri could draw beautiful and elegant geometric patterns by hand now, but the question of his survival hung by a thread. Could those patterns truly evoke ancient protection...? Msafiri wondered as he found a branch that could barely support his rest. He stared into the seemingly unchanging starry night and recalled another memory.

Legend has it that this fish bore a map on its scales. Follow it, and you would find a treasure — though what that treasure was depended entirely on what the seeker wanted most at that very moment. Suddenly, the hunger in his stomach dissolved, and all Msafiri wanted was to go home. The fish swam cheerfully in the water and responded to his wish by guiding the lost boy back home. Finally, after passing three river forks, Msafiri spotted several worried figures in the distance. Thank goodness the legend of the Guide Fish holds true, he thought and collapsed from exhaustion before he could crack a smile. The last thing he heard might have been the sound of a fish leaping out of water, but for the first time in his life, Msafiri dismissed it as a mere hallucination of his keen, reliable ears. The coming-of-age celebration finally commenced, and Msafiri received gifts from the Driftingale Guild — a backpack full of travel supplies and a half-written field guide. Someone still remembered that little boy who rushed to answer the phone call, it seemed. Though Msafiri wondered... why did the fish soup at the bonfire party that night taste a bit too salty?

His empty stomach had been growling all the way, and had there been any fish in the water, they'd all be startled and scattered by now.
Msafiri rested near the bank and peered closely at the water's surface.

Under the silvery moon, a small patch of odd scale patterns appeared before him. It almost looked like... a map?

It was the Guide Fish!

Unbeknownst to him, the note he'd left under a cup before leaving had been whisked away by the wind. After fruitless searches around the territory, his friends and family, who were all there for his coming-of-age ceremony, soon mobilized to track down the rebellious young Msafiri.

As night fell and the air cooled down, Msafiri set out once more to find proper sustenance. He wouldn't allow himself to share meals with vultures again.
As he twitched his ears and shook his head, trying to shake off unpleasant memories from yesterday, he heard the sound of flowing water from ahead.
Perhaps he could try his luck at catching fish? In the worst case, he could still drink his fill — Now was hardly the time to be concerned over catching a cold from getting wet.

Under the dim moonlight, the savanna lay shrouded in a pale silver haze. A cluster of tiny figures huddled together, their voices rising in lively chatter.

"It's my turn! What should we do tonight?"
"Hey, that's not right! It's my turn today! I'm going fishing!"
"But you get the next two days, too. That's totally unfair!"
"Well, whose fault is that? You weren't even here when it was your turn... Besides, I need to practice my hunting."
"Let me have it! The tumbleweeds are rolling today, and I'm gonna chase down the biggest one!"
"Hey, hey, cut it out! Same rule as always — let's draw lots!"

On the 364th day of his fourteenth year, Msafiri became a "runaway" on the eve of his adulthood.

He still remembered that phone call from Driftingale Guild years ago, which wasn't meant for him, but still...
It quietly planted the seed of a dream that hot summer afternoon, one of measuring every planet and every islet with his own eyes, ears, and feet. And where better to start than the very place that he called home?

Msafiri chose the perfect day to set out, with the intention of making this his very own special coming-of-age gift.
However, trials were afoot for these nascent dreams and their dreamer. And just like that, Msafiri lost his way.
The lack of experience and days of roughing it in the wilderness had taught Msafiri harsh lessons. He'd never felt this challenged back when he hunted with his parents and little brother. Only now did he realize that he wasn't quite the skilled hunter he thought himself to be out here on the plains, let alone finding directions, plotting routes, or setting up camp... All that condensed theory and knowledge in textbooks proved painfully shallow when the time came for him to apply them.
But the scorching sun had no sympathy for those beneath its rays. Msafiri huddled in a patch of tree shade, too hungry to find rest. He took out his notebook and began scribbling down everything he'd seen in the past few days.

The stars were silent. Msafiri felt as though he was under the watch of tender eyes. Beautiful memories weren't meant to be traps on his unwritten journey. They should be the strength that keeps him moving forward. Msafiri finally climbed down the tree. This is not the end yet, he thought to himself. And to his delight, another passing wind brought him the scent of prey.

The greenhorn was at a loss after causing the major blunder as Msafiri pulled out his all-purpose tape and started mending the tent.
"This is perfect. I've heard about this thing called sand bath therapy. Should we all give it a go? Kula bata!" he suggested.

That night, the entire team enjoyed a nice, long, three-hour "sand bath." Topics from serious expedition work to not-so-serious gossip were exchanged, and the newly assembled team became fast acquaintances in no time.

While the windswept sands didn't exactly have any real therapeutic properties, at the very least, some of his team felt relieved. And for Msafiri, that was all that mattered.

"Well then, welcome to Planet D-18's exploration site. I'm your Driftingale Exploration Team Guide, Msafiri."
He abducted an innocent emergency flashlight from somewhere to serve as a microphone while skillfully mimicking a documentary host.

"As you can see — we've just been invited to an exceptionally warm welcome ceremony fresh out of the vehicle, and even sampled some local delicacies."
"Pfft—" the cameraman barely stifled a giggle.

Msafiri tactfully stepped out of frame, leaving the recording to the professionals as he turned his attention to setting up camp.

This was the first time Msafiri had tasted such authentic... sand.
He spat a couple of times as he stood up. Fine yellow grains rustled and slipped free with his movements.
The camera's lens cap had just come off, capturing the localized sandstorm in full.
"So it's already started?" Msafiri leaned in, blowing away the misbehaving feathers in his hair that kept drifting into his line of sight.

The camera bobbed up and down, as if nodding in place of its operator.

Before Msafiri could put two and two together, the little rascal who had drawn the lucky lot rushed up to him. "Big bro Radar Ears! What are we gonna do? Hunting? Chase tumbleweed? Whatever it is, I'm your little brother for today!" "You're my... little brother? What do you mean?" Msafiri looked down at the kid with pigtails and expectant eyes. His lips twitched as even more questions popped into his head. "Well, anyone who draws the lucky lot can be your little brother for a day for the price of one fish! I've already paid mine~!" As the answer dawned on him, Msafiri lifted his head and twitched his ears as he spotted his actual little brother sneaking away. Uh-oh, busted! His little brother, who hadn't gone far, shuddered as the gravity of getting caught red-pawed by Msafiri descended on him. Finally, Msafiri learned why his little brother, who usually complained about never having enough fish to eat, had been sharing half of the catch lately.

"Weren't you guys supposed to take turns? Why are you here?"
"Taking turns just doesn't work. Drawing lots is way easier! Besides, I got lucky, hehe. Can't blame me for that!"
"Well, fine! You know the rules, show me the good stuff first..."

...

Could it be that his little brother was involved in something written in the sacred laws...?

And as this was happening, Msafiri was going about his usual hunting practices with his younger brother, blissfully unaware of the shenanigans that were about to unfold. His bright, sharp eyes focused intently on the prey mid-flight.
He crouched and sprang up in a clean pounce. The soft feathers landed in his palms right on cue, and so did the prey's small form. His little brother clapped in celebration.

"Plop!" said the small pebble that suddenly struck his brother's back. Msafiri immediately locked onto the source of this prank with deadly precision. He was on his way to teach the little troublemaker a lesson when his brother spoke up.
"It's fine! That was our signal, heh."

He watched as his brother skipped toward the "secret meeting" and kept watch from a respectful distance. Even kids need their privacy, he thought to himself.
However, whether it was the telltale winds or the rush of excitement after a successful hunt, Msafiri's sensitive ears overheard some strange chatter.

One of them reached into a pocket and pulled out a fistful of small wooden chips. In an instant, the others swarmed in, each snatching a piece.

"The triangle mark — I got it!" someone cheered, letting out a triumphant whistle, while the others could only pout and grumble, tossing their blank chips back onto the pile.

But the camera faithfully captured everything in sight, including a greenhorn who accidentally tore a hole in the tent just as another wave of yellow sand came with a gust of wind.

Fortunately, this one came and went quickly, and Msafiri's timely assisted evacuation meant that no one was hurt.
No one, except for the torn tent, now half-filled with sand.

"His Highness Diannan departed for his homeland, seen off by the Chancellor... □□□□□ May the Sovereign live forever like the Sun God, rich and healthy... His Highness was assassinated at the Step Cascade..."

"Year 19, second month of Winter, 5th day, □□□ cruel lion, □□ city-state, □□□□ temple □□ sacrifice... Raging fire swallowed □□□□□... □□ juice like human blood, added to the wine..."

"Year 20, second month of □, □7th day, the 9□th day of the Sovereign's illness... □□ priest violated the Queen's □□, sought audience with the Sovereign, and presented a golden dagger... That Sovereign, went calmly mad... May the Sovereign live forever like the Sun God, rich and healthy"

"Year 19, first month of summer, 4th day. Celebration of the King's Coronation. Envoys from all states arrived at the Golden City."

"The foreign leaders crawled forward, kissing the soil to show submission to the King's majesty... offering gold, silver, sapphires, emeralds... □□□ wine and livestock for the King's troops... offering the children of princes."

"Year 19, first month of summer, 11th day. The last day of the celebration. His Highness Dianan of □□ came for the marriage alliance □□... grateful for the King's ceasefire, □□□□□□ making new clothes... The King praised His Highness's sincerity and had formal wear custom-made for him..."

...

"Year 19, first month of autumn, 2nd day. The Papyrus River stopped flowing, and the fields yielded nothing. The marriage between the Queen and the High Priest □□ was not blessed by the Sun God."

"The Sovereign's victory is sung in □□, his glory and deeds □□ manifest, known to all in □□, high and low..."

...

"...I have marked my boundaries, willing... born to be king. Anyone who abandons the glory of □□ and refuses to struggle... is not a destined sovereign... Take this as motivation and wage war on its behalf."

"Dedicated to the great and powerful... For him, the sun shines, bestowing life and true love."

"The King □□ war, □□ army, □□ the topsy-turvy world, □□□□ every suffering city, bringing the Sun God's gift, bringing life."

"...Allowing the King's subjects to take grain, allowing widows and □□ to take grain □□□□ to give to the hungry. In the King's □□□□ no one shall die from this again."

"The poor become rich, and the slaves rejoice. □ status □□ is abolished. The people have taken up arms, following the Son of the Sun God, □□ eternal King."

"...2,500 chariots crossed the stream near □□□, launching a charge. Prince □□□'s army was setting up camp, receiving no warning. The army □□ betrayed him."

"He rose swiftly, like the furious Sun God... took up arms, □ on armor, □□ God of Strength, annihilating the leader and the entire army of □□□□. Their infantry and cavalry fell at Prince □'s feet."

"Prince □□ drove the enemy army out of the territory, □□ falling into the river one by one like crocodiles... □□□□ attacking all enemies..."

"Harvis knew the two Princes □□□ would triumph, for a true monarch fears not death, □□ resurrection, that is the God of the Underworld."

"□□□ The river has run dry... The sands are waterless, the riverbeds waterless, the earth is in chaos and disorder"

"□□□ dying of starvation... Someone □□□□□ children... barely clothed, □□□□ invading our home, like hungry locusts, □□□□ standing with the foreign enemy, exploiting the King's subjects... The sky is shrouded in the storms of the underworld"

"Year 27, the first month of Summer, day 10. The King once again ascended his golden chariot, clad in shining armor, like the Sun God... the master of the battlefield"

"Year 10, Second Month of Spring, 10th Day. Havis arrived at the Golden City. □□ revelation from the Sun God. The Queen's □□. □□ teacher to the two Princes."

"The High Priest prophesied that a demon would be born among the □□□ Princes... The □ Prince was born with an eye ailment. Havis believed the monarch had the Sun God's protection... appreciated the □□ Prince, taught him earnestly."

...

"Year 15, First Month of Autumn, 4th Day. Havis gave lessons to the Little Prince and the First Prince at court."

He heard a sound emerge from the silence—faint, spirited, like a feather landing on water, like a soul flying towards the sky, like dew melting into the air.
"Hmm? A new follower..."
He opened his eyes and looked at the person on the other side of the pillar of fire. The silence burned within the blaze, creating the sound of a heartbeat.

You place the golden dagger on the scales. Hmm? I have passed judgment and been reborn. So... why have you awakened me?
That familiar look in your eyes... it's as if you have been watching me for a very, very long time...
"Who seeks an audience?"

He would still see the desert of the ancient kingdom, the flooding green rivers flanked by fields of golden wheat, and the sweet scent of fig trees.
Only the temples of the gods lay in ruin, overgrown with Wildgrass, as if they had never existed, turned into roads for common folk to tread.
Beyond that, nothing remained.
Around the decay, boundless and bare, the lone and level sands stretched far away.

The heart he could not find was scattered among the stars along with his memories.
The judgment prepared for him could never begin... Judge me? Ridiculous.
He traveled to and fro with the boat, rising and setting with the sun, in an endless cycle until the end... When is the end?
The pitch-black messenger on the boat bowed piously behind him, telling him his time had come.

He walked through an endless dream.
The wind brushed past his tightly closed eyes, falling into the boundless reeds without a sound—silence.
He opened his eyes and looked ahead. Countless souls flapped their wings, flying towards the land of bliss. Their hearts were pure and light, like feathers.
But he raised his hand, signaling the deity behind him to stop advancing.
His boat passed through raging fire, traversed the gates of countless deities, reached this field of reeds, and stopped once again.
In the place where the sun shines, all souls yearn for the future, but he is merely a traveler.

The golden mask on his face has pursed lips and knitted brows, exuding incomparable majesty.
Thousands of trials did not shatter the young monarch's arrogance: "I am the King of Kings."
The carver must have deeply understood the monarch's emotions: "My King's achievements surpass all things; the strong bow before him."

"Prince □ disobeyed his □□□□ teacher... I wish for my people to □□ own land, have □□ warmth and food, and fear no foreign enemies... Those of status are not permitted to □□ land."

"Havis □□ the Prince's remarks, worried that the Queen □□, □□ the First Prince admonished □□□ that one must not □□□□, so as to avoid □□ disaster."

"The First Prince... was once again confined by the Queen for insubordination and speaking recklessly... Havis's admonishment was unsuccessful; Prince □ was imprisoned for □□ days, until the evil □□ city-state attacked."

"Prince □ boarded the golden chariot symbolizing the monarch, assisted by Prince □ and Havis... The army gathered □□, successively □□□□ city-states."

The answer came logically as the girl casually picked up a conch shell on the beach. "Just put this conch and that hermit crab and the other big seashells in your pocket. If you have a bunch of them, you won't get blown away by the wind anymore. I mean, I've never seen a hermit crab get toppled by a breeze."

"There's always a way to stay, as long as you want to stay," the girl said. "That's how it goes."

The hermit crab poked its head out of the shell and, realizing it was wobbling around in someone's pocket, quietly retreated back inside. Nerina stood in a daze. There's always a way to stay, as long as I want to stay. Last time, she wanted to leave, so she set off and came to land. But this time, she wanted to stay, so she clutched the shells in her hand tightly and readied herself for a second "departure."

"What's on your mind?" The girl took Nerina's hand and led her forward. "Let's go to the mayor's house in a bit. I heard he has something like a kerosene lamp, called a lightbulb!"
"Lightbulb?"
"It's really bright, like, way brighter than the lamps!"
"Brighter than... fire?"
"Even brighter than fire!"
"Then it's... very dangerous. We should stay away. Otherwise, it'll dry us out."

Nerina huddled in the shadows of the deck as the tour boat sailed past the desolate island. The tour guide's commentary crackled through the loudspeakers while scattered tourists showed little interest in this particular site.

"Ladies and gentlemen, if you would look to your right, following the direction of the boat, you'd see a seemingly unremarkable island. It was the cradle of an ancient civilization..."

"Could you take a photo for me, dearie?" A gray-haired traveler held out her camera at Nerina. Nerina hesitated for a moment, then quietly took it from her.
"Okay."

It's changed so much, she thought to herself. The place she once called home had become an archaeological preserve, and not even she could come and go as she pleased anymore. A long gaze while passing by on a tour boat was all she had now.

From the corner of her eyes, Nerina glimpsed a group of young girls embracing before a cascade of flowers in the photograph, smiling at the camera.
"She'll never hear the song now."
"...People always leave."
"Yes," Harper removed her glasses and closed her eyes in the warmth of the sun. "People always do."
"Nothing ever stays."

"So you want to stay, but you're too light. The wind would carry you away." The girl with pigtails nodded.
Nerina breathed a sigh of relief. The explanations were long and complicated, and as she explained, the girl kept adding even more questions, leaving her flustered and spinning in circles.
"Then just... make yourself heavier."

The boat honked as it slowly drifted away from the island.
Harper had fallen asleep, her breathing gradually becoming shallow and steady. Nerina slipped away from her and hurried to the stern of the deck. She pulled a pearl from her pocket. Beneath its honey-colored luster, a melody seemed to breathe and pulse within.
Clay tablets would get drenched, paper would dry out and crumble to dust. Nerina had searched long and hard, and in the end, only pearls could hold those precious moments in time.

As she plucked the lyre strings, the sky seemed to darken. The bonfire on the beach in her memory flickered, its warm glow blurring Maria's smiling face, but her voice remained crystal clear. Nerina could hear her again, "So you're saying, bonfires have melodies too? What do they sound like?" "Bloop, let me sing it for you." Nerina began to sing the song. Together, the two of them sang the song once more. Their voices and the lyre's melody made ripples through time, travelling from the island of yesteryear to the boat in the present before finally landing warmly back onto the sea. The memories remain, the island remains, and I remain... Nerina thought to herself. Nothing ever stays, but in the music they will remain. Forever.
"Mama, look! The fishies are swimming over!"

"...Through systematic excavation of the ruins, archaeologists discovered inscriptions on the unearthed clay tablets that strongly resembled modern sheet music..."

Harper seemed like a genuinely friendly old lady. She smiled warmly and sat down beside Nerina, "This isn't exactly the most popular tourist route. Are you here alone?"
"...No, with friends. Together. Coming back for a visit."

"Oh, to be young." Harper shakily pulled out a black-and-white photograph from her pocket. Slipping on her reading glasses, she pored over it intently. "A long time ago, when I was still a young girl, my friend and I made a promise that one day, we'd come here together to listen to these ancient melodies. They say that when the music plays, a divine spectacle appears above the sea. Haha, isn't that fascinating?"
"...Mm."
"Such a pity she passed on before I did."

"Why aren't you answering me?"
"I... don't know either."
"What do you mean you don't know?!" The drooped pigtails sprang back up. "You don't have a destination? No plan?"
"When the wind comes, I'll go. I can't stop."

Nerina had no way to hide from the "currents" on land. When the wind comes, she'd be lifted into the clouds. And when the wind stops, she'd drift slowly back down.
But the girl couldn't understand. She leaned in close, warmth radiating from her as she blinked with curious eyes, "What do you mean?"

"...Based on recent archaeological findings, we can confirm that a highly organized human settlement existed here at least three thousand years ago and vanished following a volcanic eruption..." The loudspeakers continued.

After the flash went off, the traveler named Harper smiled cheerfully at the photo of herself and the island and said, "Isn't it marvelous? My age is nothing compared to the island. To it, I am but a child."
"Mm." Nerina agreed and curled back into the shadows. Even with the moist sea breeze, the midday sun had left her feeling more than a bit parched.
She squinted at the faraway island that looked like an emerald gem pinned to the surface of the ocean.

Beneath the brilliant sunset, on the soft golden sands, a cheerful melody from a lyre can be heard.
"Boop~ Bloop-boop~ boop-bloop, boop~"
A little girl with pigtails danced to the tune. When the song ended, her hair bounced with the applause.

"What's this song about?"
"Maria and I making pottery, picking olives, and eating grapes together."
"Ooh~ It must all happened on a beautiful sunny day, right?"
"...Bloop."
"That sounds wonderful! What about ours? If you wrote a song about me fixing your lyre today, what would it sound like?"

Nerina didn't need long to think. The strings vibrated once more, and the melody came. Opening with a light and gleeful tune for the serendipitous discovery of seashells, the melody softened into careful, bouncing notes that told the delicate work of the girl's repair on the lyre, before finally slowing into a bittersweet goodbye.

"Wait, you mean... you're leaving?!"
The girl with pigtails clutched Nerina's arm, her hair standing on end. "Where are you going? When are you planning to leave? How? We've only just become friends! Do you really have to go so soon? Are you going home? I don't even know where you live..."

The questions came rapid-fire, one after another, and Nerina felt like she was back underwater again — tiny bubbles bursting all around her, sounds layering and overlapping until her little head was overwhelmed.

storytitle: Stars at Just the Right Warmth
text:
The soft sound of currents breaking into tiny bubbles filled the space around her, and Nerina knew she was no longer alone in the coral grove.

"What are you looking at?"
"The stars."

The sky was always there above, and the stars could be seen even from the ocean floor. When night fell, Nerina watched their "starlight" shimmer across the waves.

Orange like the sun, yet not as vast or as daunting. She thought with relief that maybe the stars, of all things, were just the right warmth. "Those are human torches." Her companion said and turned away. The soft hem of their garment swayed in the water, and the waves in the wake of their departure bobbed Nerina up and down. Even so, she kept her gaze upward, watching as the "starlight" drifted closer, then slowly away again. "Tor... ches." The word lingered in Nerina's mind like a melody, yet she couldn't form its shape. What are torches? And what do they sound like...? Her companion had already left the grove, leaving only a trail of bubbles behind. The bubbles carried a message, urging her on: "Hurry. You'll be late for class." It's not my fault that composition is so boring. Nerina plucked at the lyre strings while spacing out. Nobody really wanted to be there for the dull lesson. A coral pointer struck her lyre, breaking her out of her reverie. Seeing the teacher about to puff up like a frustrated balloon, Nerina quickly raised her hand to rejoin the orchestra's melody — a tedious, solemn, and weighty piece as slow as a sea turtle. All raised hands in the classroom then descended onto the strings in gentle, graceful arcs. Sometimes pausing for a second, other times much longer, long enough for a tiny planula to mature into a massive coral. Only after such an agonizingly long wait would the next note of the section slowly emerge. This was the same section where Nerina almost passed out from holding her breath during the previous rehearsal. And when the next note finally came, she nearly drowned herself again with deep, desperate inhales. She refused to move her hand again, because she couldn't fathom the meaning behind the piece. Maybe it was about an old sea turtle taking a stroll, or even the lives of seahorses, who were often motionless between the corals. In any case, it certainly wasn't a hymn that praised and celebrated the gift of joy from the Ocean God, as her teacher had claimed.

Icy-cold seawater births icy-cold music. Then... where does one find warm, rich, and delightful music?
Nerina tilted her head upward once again, at the sky forever above. When night fell, starlight would shimmer on the waves. Orange "stars," swaying like tiny little suns.
The music she was looking for was on land.

"Time: Allegro"
"Weather: Scorching"
"A few days ago, at night, I took the lyre and swam toward the stars on the ocean's surface, but a torrent appeared and carried me far away."

"Dizzy and unconscious. When I woke up, I was on the beach."
"This is my first time... on land."

"Nerina!" The teacher glided over. "What in the waters are you thinking about?"
"I'm thinking... is this what music is supposed to sound like?"
"What do you mean 'is supposed to sound like'? What are you trying to say?" The teacher swelled up another size, rolling furiously around Nerina. "Of COURSE this is what music sounds like!"
"But it's so slow and silent."
"Isn't that exactly how the ocean is?"
"And it sounds so... cold."
"The seawater IS cold!"
Ah... Nerina supposed her teacher had a fair point.

"Those on land like to press against each other warmly. They say it's called a hug, a ritual for becoming friends."
"Maria is... my friend. I don't quite understand what 'friend' means, but I broke a clay pot that humans cherish, and she didn't mind."

"She took me to see the bonfire. The melody of fire was very pleasant. It's a... warmth that didn't exist in the sea. Maria couldn't hear it, so I played it for her. She loved it and danced along with the song. We sat by the bonfire for a long, long time."

"But I can't get too close to the fire. Hair and hands... will dry out."
"I wanted to stay moisturized with seawater, but Maria wouldn't let me lie in the waves. She's right... I get swept away easily, and I don't want to leave yet. So I ended up bursting another big clay pot with water. Maria wasn't angry, because she is... my friend."
"I like having friends. And I like being on land. Next time, I must remember to get a bigger pot."
— A clay tablet covered in tadpole-shaped writing

storytitle: A Tune and a Hermit Crab in the Wind
text:
"Time: Adagio"
"Weather: Pleasant"
"This place is always raining. Sometimes I take out the old clay tablets, and they often get wet. I've transcribed memories from the days I spent with Maria and my other friends onto paper, but paper doesn't last long either..."
"Can these melodies really be preserved?..."
"..."

"It feels like not much time has passed since I first stepped onto land, but truth is, I'm already so very far away from that first island."
"The wind will pick up in a few days, and when it does, I'll drift to a new place, even though I don't want to say goodbye to my new friends yet..."
"..."
"Maybe I should... repair the lyre before I leave."
— A unfinished sheet of music

"Everything is different here. The air feels dense, the sounds are rich, and the water is thin. Without water's protection, the sun is scorching."
"There are people living on land. The sounds of their voices are... unlike any melody I've ever heard."
"And there are so many other melodies, too. Wind rustling through treetops, waves lapping against rocky shores, butterflies spreading their wings, and beetles strolling across the grass..."
"I want to remember every single note."

And yet, Mo Ji soon began a strange kind of "communication" between them.
Whenever Harpeno deliberately went against the navigator's instructions, venting a frustration she couldn't quite name, a new map would appear in her locker the next day. Every wrong turn was marked in red, with a small stick figure doodled beside it, fuming with anger. She would scribble "Mind your own business" across the page. In reply, Mo Ji would sketch a girl covering her ears in the corner, neatly labeled: "Signal reception weak."

Gradually, Harpeno came to realize that Mo Ji's maps were more than routes. They were a language of their own. Color intensity indicated the severity of obstacles. Line weight marked their size. Vivid, concrete depictions made it easy to see what would otherwise be hard to picture. This was not something taught in textbooks. It was a private code, entirely her own.

The turning point came during the feared stardust belt navigation exam before graduation.
As Harpeno approached the target zone, the navigator began to glitch, and every instrument flickered wildly. Amidst the chaos at the exam control center, Mo Ji burst in, took the communicator, and made herself heard for the first time in three years—
"Trust your eyes, Harpeno!" Her voice was hoarse but steady. "Half a turn right. That nebula ahead isn't real. It's a debris field! Trust me. You can see it."
Harpeno held her breath. Her gaze pierced through the interference, and sure enough, there was a hidden safe passage. Mo Ji had already mapped the area in greater detail than any navigation system could. And in that moment, she chose to trust Harpeno's eyes over every instrument.

"Are you pitying me?" She crumpled the map into a ball and tossed it back at Mo Ji. "I don't need directions from someone who can't even speak."
Mo Ji didn't get angry. She picked up the crumpled map, smoothed it out, then drew a large question mark on the back and held it out to her.
Harpeno let out a helpless laugh. In that instant, she knew she had gone too far.
"Sorry."
She left the word behind and turned away, eager to put an end to the conversation before it slipped any further out of her control.

During Harpeno's final year at the Transit Academy, she was on the edge of erupting like a volcano every single day. Her hawkeyes could pierce through nebulas with ease, but she couldn't remember how to get from the lecture hall to the cafeteria to save her life.
"Worthless!" She slammed the electronic navigator onto the bench in frustration. "Did they design the path with their eyes closed?!"

A folded piece of paper slid to her feet. On it was a hand-drawn campus map, with each path marked by unique visual landmarks. "Turn left at the rusted car shell," "go straight past the café with the pigeon cage," and "turn right at the yellow-hatted scarecrow." The directions were precise, but peculiar.

She looked up and saw Mo Ji, the campus "weirdo" rumored to have not spoken a word in three years.
Mo Ji stared silently at her with eyes as calm as deep space.

On their way back, Chen gazed up at the sky of stars and said, "Remember this feeling. Rules are the backbone of the Starsea, but those who enforce them need to know what they're fighting for. You did the right thing today. You held the line and left room for compassion."

That night, Harpeno added a new entry to her log: "The Starsea needs order, but also, compassion."
She carefully folded the stub of the ticket for "No. 50" and tucked it away. Her uniform remained pressed and straight, yet somewhere between its rigid lines, Harpeno found a gentle give quietly forming.

Harpeno could hear a dispassionate voice reciting Article 38 of the Starsea Navigation Safety Act in her mind: Decommissioned vehicles are strictly prohibited on routes. But the big, dewy eyes of the furry little ones stared right through the voice and into her heart. "Write the ticket." Chen's voice fell without hesitation. Just as Harpeno was about to tear off the ticket, she paused and added, "Recommending referral to an animal shelter." "But, my shipment..." "You're an adult, so take responsibility for your actions like one," Harpeno didn't hesitate. "The cargo will be held in storage. Once the penalty is complete, you may retrieve it with a compliant vehicle." Lee accepted the ticket with eyes welling with tears.

She examined and read out the data, "Your actual mileage exceeded the allowed maximum by 40%, and the engine is severely deteriorated. You're lucky that it hasn't led to graver consequences." She looked toward the cargo hold, where countless puppies, kittens, along with a few long-haired rabbits and call ducks, scattered haphazardly among the shipment. The long journey had already left several of them looking queasy, but to Harpeno's surprise, the temperature inside the was quite comfortable, and the space was clean with hardly any odor.
"They're all strays I picked up along the way. If I'd left them outside in this weather, they probably wouldn't make it..." Lee's voice grew quieter and quieter.

In her new uniform, neatly pressed and rigid as the iron clauses of the law, Harpeno began her probationary patrol under Instructor Chen.

Cargo truck "No. 50" lay wheezing on the roadside greenery, puffing white smoke and barely hanging on. Its driver, Lee, rubbed his hands nervously and explained, "It's nothing, just a minor malfunction..."
Harpeno's detector began blaring.

"YOU'RE INSANE!!!" He screamed.
"Now you know who catches the wind," she replied nonchalantly. "The black hole."
Harpeno's eyes and mind calculated the vehicle's trajectory with precision. When the drunk driver's survival instincts finally forced him to hit the brakes, she was already there to greet him at the only exit with a tap on his window.

"Two hundred percent over the speed limit, and driving under the influence to boot," she handed over the digital ticket. "You've just set a new record for violations in five years, and unfortunately, you'll be paying for your recklessness for the next five to come."

After the heart-racing, sobering chase, the man accepted the ticket with a ghastly white face. In that moment, the entire Starsea could hear the sound of his engine dying.

Just then, an ambulance siren began to wail in the distance, but it wasn't getting any closer — it was stuck at the very back of the queue.
"Everyone, clear the way!" Harpeno suddenly raised her voice. She jumped onto the roof of the nearest vehicle and held up her megaphone and body camera. "Listen up, everyone! Left three lanes move forward in order, right two lanes stay put. Blue cargo truck, move two car lengths to the right — yes, you! Anyone who refuses to follow instructions can kiss their license goodbye!"
Her commands were clear, assertive, and indisputable.

This was Harpeno's first time handling rush hour on her own. Three cargo trucks created a complete gridlock at the intersection while fighting for the right of way, and a long line of angry, honking vehicles stretched behind them. A few drivers leaned against their doors, pontificating about the day's big Starsea news, and couldn't care less when they saw Harpeno's patrol car approaching.

"Little lady, get your supervisor," a stubbly-faced truck driver waved dismissively at her. "This isn't the place to play house."
Harpeno was silent. Her boot heels clicked against the pavement as she walked straight between the three deadlocked trucks.
"First truck." She pointed at the stubbly-faced driver's vehicle. "Your transport permit expired three months ago."
She turned to the next two trucks and continued, "Second truck, you're overloaded. Third truck, your right rear brake light is out."
She swiftly wrote out three tickets to follow.
"Now," she looked up. "Do I need to teach you gentlemen how to reverse, too?"
The three drivers' expressions immediately changed.
"Do you have any idea what we're hauling? You think you can afford to pay for the delay?"
"I certainly can't, but I can make you pay a whole lot more." She waved her ticket book. "Want to try me?"

That day, the Starsea was as clogged up as Monday mornings during rush hour. The senior patrol officers all exchanged knowing glances in the break room, their eyes full of unspoken implications.
"Hey, rookie—" The captain pointed to the new face in the corner.

The other patrol officers began whispering among themselves.
"That one couldn't even find her way two hundred meters outside the rest area last month."
"Oy, can't have them say that we're picking on a girl now."
"Right, then you get out there."
"Nope!"
"Alright rookie, consider this your orientation. You're up." The captain made his decision.

After clocking out for the day, Harpeno went home and made herself a cup of coffee. Outside her window, the Starsea remained clamorous, but every route ran with orderly discipline. She tapped her fingertips lightly against the cup.
"And that's the way a peaceful night should be."

"Enough with the theatrics," A cold voice cut in. "You look more like a monkey swinging between branches."
Eyes watched as Harpeno's patrol bike eclipsed the sky like a chromatic cloud of divine punishment, hot on the wheels of the speeding ball of flame.

The drunk driver laughed amidst the flames and slammed the throttle to the floor. The two vehicles then became tangled trails of light on a chase across the Starsea. The rulebreaker thought he had the upper hand until he realized Harpeno was intentionally driving him toward a dust lane in the Starsea, a place where even signals couldn't escape.

Everyone in the Starsea calls her the "Tyrant."
Harpeno loves the nickname. Her patrol bike is the needle that passes between Starsea routes and stitches unruly vehicles back into the traffic network of order.

One day, some young aristocrat with a souped-up ride painted with flame decals smashed through a parking sign at the Galactic Bazaar. "I am the WIND! No one can catch the WIND!" He hollered. His drunken laughter was insufferably pompous as he sped away, and every public LED screen across the Starsea lit up to cover this chaotic spectacle.

When the exam concluded, Harpeno found Mo Ji. "Why did you...?"
"My parents were Starsea cartographers," Mo Ji wrote slowly across the page. "They lost their way in the Starsea for lack of accurate charts, and never returned. I map the Starsea so no one else will be lost to the unknown. And you are..." She paused. "You're the only person I've ever met who can verify all my charts with the naked eye. I need your sight."

She did not see Harpeno as someone in need of saving. She was simply looking for someone to walk the same path.

The drivers who'd been onlookers up until now instinctively obeyed her words. When someone tried to cut in line, a single icy glare from Harpeno was enough to discourage their attempt and put them back in their place.
Gradually, the hopeless knot of traffic began to loosen. When the ambulance finally passed through, the drivers spontaneously honked their horns — the way Starsea drivers give thanks.
"Nice work, Miss 'Tyrant'!"
Nobody knew who started it, but everyone agreed that the nickname was a perfect fit for their decisive, no-nonsense new patrol officer.

The captain was waiting for Harpeno by the door after the team wrapped up debriefing.
"You've become the talk of all Starsea drivers after your battle today." He said.
"Hungry."
"Come again?" The captain had to clean out his ear. He could've sworn he just heard Harpeno meow like a cat.
"Are we getting barbecue or hot pot?" Harpeno flopped onto the lounge chair, seemingly drained. "Energy level critical."
Soft laughter rang out behind her as the senior officers exchanged new looks with each other. This time, feeling much closer to their new colleague.

At graduation, Mo Ji gave Harpeno one final Starsea chart.
"I'm going to finish what they started," Mo Ji said, "And you'll go on to build your own order."

Years later, the name of the Starsea Tyrant had spread far and wide, yet Harpeno never saw Mo Ji again. In the depths of her heart, however, there would always be a serene stretch of stars reserved for a certain "Starwhisperer."
